At which point does a game stop being a game? How much of player interaction do you have to take away? Goals and win states? Rules and constraints? Game over screens and credits roll?

That's an excellent point, especially coming off the heels of your earlier post about That Dragon, Cancer devs and let's play videos. I think every new type of game has a period of novelty and over-saturation. Good genres will carry on with quality and you'll see one or two notable titles retain their popularity, but sometimes a genre of games just doesn't have the mainstream appeal necessary to keep it relevant for long.

Truth be told, I'm scared of the mainstream appeal and what's doing to the industry as a whole. Games and entire genres are being streamlined and simplified to the point of destroying any depth, complexity, challenge just to make a quick buck. Why would anyone prefer Everybody's Gone to the Rapture over Firewatch for instance?

Reducing barrier of entry for production was the cause of lost interest for games in the US back in the 80s. You had shovelware everywhere. Now we have a double peril. Reducing the barrier of entry for developers as well the audience. Why would people buy games if they don't require you to develop any kind of skill? Whether it's reflexes and hand-to-eye coordination or deep and strategical thinking skills? You don't have games anymore, just a bland copy-paste sludge of boredom.

I think that will be some seriously disruptive shit in the years ahead, and the devs and publishers will have no one to blame but themselves. Of course they will blame "the entitled gamer" instead. And keep wondering why people prefer to watch games on Youtube instead of playing them. Shit times now, shittier times ahead.
